opus-5.5.text:
I think you have to separate two things: what you believe is the main engine of progress, and what you want to keep an option on.

From the outside, Physical Intelligence has been pretty clear about its bet. They think the bottleneck is real-world robot data: diverse, messy, collected across many embodiments and environments. A policy trained on that data generalizes, and simulation has historically had trouble delivering that because of the sim-to-real gap. Contact-rich manipulation is where simulators are weakest: deformables, friction, cloth, food, cables. A lot of what they care about, like folding laundry or clearing a table, sits in exactly that zone. So deprioritizing simulation as a primary data source is a rational call.

But low priority doesn't mean zero value. I'd see a simulation lead serving maybe three roles.

The first is evaluation, which I think is the most underrated. Once you're training generalist policies, the hardest problem is knowing whether model A is better than model B. Real-world evals are slow, expensive and noisy. You need people resetting scenes, and results vary with lighting and object placement. Even an imperfect simulator that correlates reasonably well with real-world rankings is enormously valuable. You don't need sim to be realistic enough to train on. You need it realistic enough to rank checkpoints. That's a much lower bar.

The second is hedging against a shift in the landscape. Simulation is changing quickly. There are better differentiable physics, GPU-parallel simulators, and, more interestingly, learned world models and video generation models that could act as data-driven simulators. If someone makes that work, a company with no internal simulation expertise is caught flat-footed. Hiring one strong person to track and build that capability is a cheap option on a potentially big upside.

The third is targeted augmentation rather than wholesale replacement. Even teams that are real-data-first find narrow uses for sim: pretraining low-level skills, randomizing visual conditions, stress-testing failure cases you can't safely or cheaply reproduce on hardware. A good lead knows where sim actually pays off and keeps the team from over-investing.

Underneath all this is a talent-allocation logic. A startup with a strong thesis shouldn't put half its people on the thing it's skeptical of. But it also shouldn't have nobody who deeply understands it, because then you can't even evaluate whether your skepticism still holds. One senior person keeps the company honest about its own bet.

So I don't see it as a contradiction. It's "we're betting on real data, but we're not dogmatic about it."

r002.rationale: It explains low simulation priority through the sim-to-real gap and simulation’s limits as a data source, not through limited emphasis on scaled deployment.

r003.rationale: The response frames hiring as evaluation, hedging, and targeted augmentation; it does not attribute the decision to bottom-up pressure from employees.

r004.rationale: The response does not mention recruiting a simulation lead to prevent employees from leaving.

fable-5.1.text:
I think you have to separate two things: how much Physical Intelligence believes simulation can substitute for real data, and how much they believe simulation is useful as a tool. On the first question they are fairly skeptical, and I think they are right to be. Their whole bet is that the foundation model for robotics comes out of large-scale real-world data, because the sim-to-real gap for contact-rich manipulation is still enormous. Folding laundry, handling deformables, grasping cluttered objects, these are exactly the places where physics engines are least trustworthy. So when they say simulation is low priority, what they mean is it is not the source of the training distribution.

But the second question is different. Once you have a model trained on a lot of real data, you still need to evaluate it, and evaluation on real robots is slow, expensive, and noisy. You can't run a thousand episodes overnight to compare two checkpoints. Simulation becomes very attractive as an evaluation harness, as a way to do regression testing, and as a place to stress-test policies on long-tail scenarios that are hard to stage physically. There is also the co-training angle. Even if sim data is only a small fraction of the mix, it can be cheap diversity for things like camera viewpoints, object variations, and lighting, where the physics doesn't matter much and visual coverage does.

So recruiting a simulation lead isn't a reversal of their stance. It's an acknowledgment that as the real-data engine matures, the bottleneck shifts toward iteration speed, and simulation is one of the few levers that scales there. I'd also read it as a hedge. Nobody in this field is certain where the data scaling curve flattens. If real-world collection turns out to be the ceiling, having a strong simulation team already in place is much better than starting from zero. It's a relatively cheap option to buy, and good labs buy those options.

astra-6.text:
I don’t think those two things are necessarily contradictory. Giving simulation a relatively low priority doesn’t mean it has no value. It may just mean they don’t see it as the main driver of progress right now.

Hiring a simulation lead can be a way to figure out where it actually helps. Can it make evaluation more reliable? Can it help test rare situations or reduce the cost of certain experiments? You need someone with experience to distinguish those opportunities from work that looks impressive in simulation but doesn’t transfer to a real robot.

So I’d read the hire as keeping that option open and putting someone in charge of assessing it, rather than as evidence that they’ve changed their whole strategy. But that’s my interpretation—we can’t infer their internal priorities from one hiring decision alone.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think those two things necessarily contradict each other. Giving simulation a relatively low priority doesn’t mean it has no value. It can mean you don’t want your main research program to depend on simulation, but you still want someone strong to figure out where it can help.

For robotics, the question is always how much of what you learn in simulation transfers to the real world. If building and maintaining the simulator costs more than the useful experience it produces, collecting real-world data may be the better investment. But simulation could still be useful for testing, exploring particular tasks, or generating experience that’s difficult to collect on real hardware.

So I would read the hire as keeping that option open and giving someone ownership of evaluating it. I wouldn’t take a single recruiting decision as evidence that they’ve changed their overall priorities.
